rationale: B wins by a hair because it turns the best tension into reporter mechanics, not just a clean line: "Bumble says women still message first. Now the AI can write the message." asks disclosure and opt-in, which is where the story gets sharp. A's "The app that made women message first will now help write the message" is the better headline, but its proof stops at "how AI assistance squares with women-message-first" instead of naming the trapdoor questions. B also adds a real hands-on lane, though calling it "customer-story" is a label in search of a fact.
gaps_in_A: "The relaunch is the founder's first big public move since returning as CEO this year" is not in the supplied facts. If that is not true, the founder angle gets wobblier fast.
"how AI assistance squares with women-message-first" is too broad. The sharper proof questions are whether AI-drafted openers are disclosed and whether the feature is opt-in or default.
"Bumble's entire brand is a single authentic human gesture" overstates the supplied facts. Strong line, but it needs support or it becomes columnist perfume.
By refusing only "The redesigned app: what's new in Bumble's interface," A misses the stronger product-access angle: have a reporter test the AI match and opener, not review the wallpaper.
gaps_in_B: "Bumble sells subscriptions" is not in the supplied update. Paying users are in-bounds; subscription mechanics need sourcing.
"the first product the returned founder has put their name on" is an invented claim unless the company can prove it. Do not smuggle chronology into a founder comeback story.

"one concrete decision the founder made in the relaunch that the previous leadership would not have made" asks for a counterfactual. Useful color, lousy proof standard unless someone will say it on record.
"What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line" is viable, but "customer-story" is the wrong label. No customer story exists here; it is a hands-on product test.
